resources.note: The Acceleration tab shows F = m a live: change the mass, keep the push, watch the acceleration.

tips.title: F = ma uses the resultant
tips.body: The $F$ in $F = ma$ is the **resultant** force, not the engine force or the push. Work out the resultant first, by subtracting friction and drag, and only then divide by the mass.

tips.title: Steady speed means zero resultant
tips.body: A car at constant velocity has driving force **equal** to the resisting forces, so the resultant is zero. Constant speed does not mean a forward resultant; that is Newton's first law.

tips.title: Which mass is accelerating?
tips.body: In a trolley-and-masses experiment the whole system accelerates, so use the **total** mass of trolley plus hanging masses. Using the trolley alone is the standard practical mistake.

tips.title: Find the resultant before the formula
tips.body: Work out the **resultant force** on its own line before going near $F = ma$. The formula takes the resultant, never the driving force alone, and separating the two steps stops the engine force being substituted while friction is still unaccounted for.

why.matters:
The three laws are the bridge between the forces on a thing and how it moves. Given the forces you can say what the motion will do; given the motion you can work out what the forces must have been. Nothing else in the course connects the two.

The first law says motion only changes when the resultant is not zero. The second puts a number on how much, with $F = ma$. The third says forces come in pairs, on **two different objects** — which is the half that gets missed, and the half that explains how anything pushes off anything.

examples.title: Why a crumple zone is not just padding
examples.body:
In a crash the car stops and, by the first law, you do not — you carry on at 13.4 m/s until something applies a force to you. How big that force is depends on how long the stopping takes.

Stop a 70 kg passenger in 0.05 s against something rigid and it takes **18.8 kN**. Spread it over 0.3 s with a belt that gives and a front end that folds, and it is **3.1 kN** — 6 times less, for the same change in speed. A crumple zone buys time, and the force falls in the same proportion.

props.caption: Same speed, same mass, six times the time

visual.alt: Two bars comparing the force on a seventy kilogram passenger stopped in five hundredths of a second against three tenths, eighteen point eight kilonewtons against three point one

examples.title: Why a rocket works with nothing to push against
examples.body:
A common objection to rockets in space is that there is nothing out there to push on. It is a fair objection and the answer is the third law: the rocket does not push on space, it pushes on its own exhaust.

The engine throws gas backwards very fast. That is a force on the gas, so the gas pushes forward on the rocket with an equal and opposite force, and the pair acts on two different objects. Air is not required anywhere in that argument — a rocket works **better** in a vacuum, because there is no drag.

props.title: Every pair acts on two different things

visual.alt: A table of three Newton third law pairs, a rocket and its exhaust, a foot and the ground, an oar and the water, each showing the two forces acting on two different objects

examples.title: Why the same car is slower with four friends in it
examples.body:
$F = ma$ says that with the force fixed, the acceleration is decided by the mass — and passengers are mass.

A 1200 kg car with a resultant of 3600 N accelerates at 3.0 m/s². Put four 70 kg people in it and the mass is 1480 kg, so the same 3600 N gives 2.43 m/s². Nought to 27 m/s stretches from 9.0 s to 11.1 s. Nothing is wrong with the engine; the force is being shared out over 1.23 times as much mass.

visual.alt: A table comparing a twelve hundred kilogram car with the same car carrying four passengers, the acceleration falling from three metres a second squared to two point four three and the time to reach twenty seven metres a second rising from nine seconds to eleven

steps.title: Newton's first law: no resultant, no change
steps.body:
**Newton's first law**: if the resultant force on an object is zero, a stationary object stays stationary and a moving object keeps moving at the same velocity, the same speed in the same direction.

So a change in velocity needs a resultant force. A car cruising at a steady 20 m/s has *balanced* forces: the driving force equals the resistive forces. To speed up, the driving force has to exceed them; to slow down, the resistive forces have to exceed the driving force.

The idea that things naturally slow down is wrong. They slow down because friction and air resistance are unbalanced forces acting on them.

visuals.alt: A free body diagram of a car with driving force 2000 N to the right and resistive forces 2000 N to the left, weight 12 000 N down and contact force 12 000 N up, with the resultant written as zero, forces balanced

check.prompt: A puck slides across frictionless ice with no resultant force on it. What happens to it?
check.solution: No resultant force means no change in velocity: the puck keeps going at the same speed in the same direction.
options: It keeps moving at the same velocity
It gradually slows down and stops
It speeds up
It stops immediately

steps.title: Velocity includes direction
steps.body:
Newton's first law is about **velocity**, not just speed. An object moving in a circle at a steady speed is changing direction all the time, so its velocity is changing, so there must be a resultant force on it. For a car on a roundabout that force is friction between the tyres and the road, pointing towards the centre. For the Moon it is gravity.

On a wet or icy road the friction is smaller, and the car cannot get the resultant force it needs to turn: it carries straight on, exactly as the first law says.

visuals.problem: A satellite orbits at a steady 7600 m/s. Is there a resultant force on it?

steps.text: Its speed is constant, but its direction keeps changing
A change in velocity needs a resultant force: Newton's first law
That force is gravity, pulling it towards the centre of the Earth

check.prompt: A car rounds a bend at a steady 15 m/s. Which is correct?
check.solution: The direction is changing so the velocity is changing, which needs a resultant force. Friction from the road provides it, towards the centre of the bend.
options: There is a resultant force in the direction it is moving
The resultant force on it is zero
There is a resultant force towards the centre of the bend
There is a resultant force away from the centre of the bend

steps.title: Newton's second law: F = m a
steps.body:
**Newton's second law**: the acceleration of an object is proportional to the resultant force on it, and inversely proportional to its mass:

$$F = m\,a$$

$F$ is the **resultant** force in N, $m$ the mass in kg, $a$ the acceleration in m/s². Recall this one; it is not on the sheet.

Double the resultant force and the acceleration doubles. Double the mass and the acceleration halves. A 1200 kg car accelerating at 2 m/s² needs a resultant force of $1200 \times 2 = 2400$ N.

visuals.alt: A card showing resultant force equals mass times acceleration, with units N, kg and m/s²

check.prompt: Calculate the resultant force needed to accelerate a 1200 kg car at 2 m/s².

steps.title: Resultant first, then acceleration
steps.body: The $F$ in $F = m a$ is the **resultant** force, never just the engine force. When a question gives several forces, find the resultant first and only then divide by the mass. Missing this step is the most common way to lose the marks.

visuals.alt: A free body diagram of a 1000 kg van with a 500 N driving force to the right and 200 N of resistive force to the left, resultant 300 N to the right

visuals.problem: A 1000 kg van has a driving force of 500 N and resistive forces of 200 N. Find its acceleration.

steps.text: The acceleration is in the direction of the resultant: forwards

check.prompt: A 12 kg sledge is pulled with 20 N while friction is 14 N. Calculate its acceleration.

steps.title: Inertia and inertial mass
steps.body:
The tendency of an object to keep doing what it is doing is called **inertia**. It is why you lurch forward when a bus brakes: the bus slows, and you keep going until the seat in front or a seat belt supplies a force.

**Inertial mass** (Higher) is a measure of how hard it is to change an object's velocity. It is defined as the ratio of force to acceleration: $m = F / a$. A bigger inertial mass needs a bigger force for the same acceleration. This is the mass in $F = m a$, and it is the same number as the mass you would weigh.

visuals.problem: A force of 60 N gives a trolley an acceleration of 4 m/s². What is its inertial mass?

steps.note: kg, the same unit as any mass

steps.text: The same trolley pushed with 120 N would accelerate at 8 m/s²
steps.note: double the force, double the acceleration

check.prompt: A resultant force of 60 N gives an object an acceleration of 4 m/s². Calculate its inertial mass.

steps.title: Required practical: force, mass and acceleration
steps.body:
Required practical 7 tests $F = m a$ with a trolley on a bench, pulled by a string over a pulley by hanging masses. Light gates connected to a data logger measure the acceleration.

**Part 1, vary the force:** keep the *total* mass constant by moving masses from the trolley to the hanger, so that the force increases but nothing else changes. Plot acceleration against force: a straight line through the origin, so $a \propto F$.

**Part 2, vary the mass:** keep the hanging mass, and so the force, constant and add masses to the trolley. Acceleration falls as mass rises: $a \propto 1/m$.

The bench can be tilted slightly to cancel friction, and the string must be horizontal.

rows: hanging mass, moved from the trolley
props.title: Required practical 7

visuals.alt: A table of the two parts of required practical 7: what is changed, what is kept the same, what is measured and the expected result

check.prompt: In the force investigation, why are masses moved from the trolley to the hanger rather than simply added to the hanger?
check.solution: The hanging masses are part of the system being accelerated. Moving them keeps the total mass constant, so only the force changes.
options: To make the trolley move faster
To keep the total mass being accelerated the same
To keep the string horizontal
To reduce friction on the bench

steps.title: Reading the practical's graph
steps.body: With total mass 0.5 kg, forces of 0.2 N to 1.0 N gave the accelerations plotted. The points lie on a straight line through the origin, so acceleration is directly proportional to force. The gradient is $a / F = 1 / m$, so the gradient of this line is $1 / 0.5 = 2$ per kg. Reading the mass off the graph like this is a favourite Higher question.

visuals.alt: A graph of acceleration against force with five points on a straight line through the origin, gradient 2, for a total mass of 0.5 kg

visuals.problem: Use the graph to find the mass of the system.

steps.text: From $F = m a$, $a = F / m$, so the gradient is $1 / m$

check.prompt: A student repeats the practical with double the total mass. How does the graph of acceleration against force change?
check.solution: Gradient is $1/m$. Doubling the mass halves the gradient; the line is still straight and through the origin.
options: It curves upwards
It becomes steeper
It no longer passes through the origin
It becomes less steep, with half the gradient

steps.title: Newton's third law: forces come in pairs
steps.body:
**Newton's third law**: whenever two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are **equal in size and opposite in direction**.

A third-law pair always has four features: same type of force, same size, opposite direction, and **acting on different objects**. Push a wall with 50 N and the wall pushes you with 50 N. A book pushes down on a table; the table pushes up on the book. The Earth pulls you down; you pull the Earth up, with the same force.

The pair is not the same thing as balanced forces. Weight and the normal contact force on a book are equal and opposite, but they both act on the book, so they are *balanced forces*, not a third-law pair.

visuals.alt: A table of third-law pairs: rocket pushes gas backwards and gas pushes rocket forwards; foot pushes ground backwards and ground pushes foot forwards; Earth pulls Moon and Moon pulls Earth; each pair the same type and size, opposite in direction, on different objects

check.prompt: A swimmer pushes backwards on the water with 80 N. What is the third-law pair force?
check.solution: Same type, same size, opposite direction, on the other object: the water pushes the swimmer forwards with 80 N. That is how swimming works.
options: The swimmer's weight of 80 N
The upthrust on the swimmer of 80 N
The water pushes the swimmer backwards with 80 N
The water pushes the swimmer forwards with 80 N

steps.title: Your turn: acceleration against force
steps.body:
Drag the resultant force on a 1000 kg car. The graph is $a = F / m$: a straight line through the origin with gradient $1/1000$. A resultant of 2500 N gives 2.5 m/s².

A typical family car can manage about 2 to 3 m/s² from rest, which is roughly 0 to 60 mph in ten seconds. An acceleration of 9.8 m/s² is a free-fall drop; a car crash can involve tens or hundreds of m/s², which is why the forces are so large.

visuals.fallback: A straight line through the origin with gradient 0.001: 1 m/s² at 1000 N, 2.5 m/s² at 2500 N and 5 m/s² at 5000 N.

check.prompt: From the graph or by calculation: a resultant force of 2500 N acts on the 1000 kg car. What is its acceleration?

steps.title: Going deeper: estimating forces, and telling the pairs apart
steps.body:
Higher tier asks you to **estimate** the forces involved in everyday motion. Start from a typical speed and time, work out the acceleration, then use $F = m a$. A 1000 kg car reaching 13 m/s (about 30 mph) in 10 s has $a = 13 \div 10 = 1.3$ m/s², so the resultant force is $1000 \times 1.3 = 1300$ N. If you are asked to *estimate*, sensible rounded values score full marks.

The other grade 9 skill is telling a **third-law pair** from **balanced forces**. Ask two questions: are the two forces on *different* objects, and are they the *same type*? Weight and the normal contact force on a resting book are both on the book and are different types, so they are balanced forces. The book's push on the table and the table's push on the book are on different objects and both contact forces: a third-law pair.

check.solution: A pair acts on two different objects and is the same type of force. Weight and the contact force both act on the book, so they are balanced forces, not a pair.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- First law: zero resultant force means no change in velocity. Stationary stays stationary; moving keeps the same speed and direction.
- Second law: $F = m a$, where $F$ is the **resultant** force. Find the resultant first.
- Inertia is the tendency to keep the same velocity; inertial mass is $F / a$.
- Required practical 7: vary force with total mass constant, then vary mass with force constant; light gates measure acceleration. $a \propto F$, $a \propto 1/m$.
- Third law: interacting objects exert equal and opposite forces of the same type on each other. A pair acts on different objects; balanced forces act on one object.
- Estimating: typical speed and time, then $a$, then $F = m a$.

questions.solution: The pair is the same type of force, same size, opposite direction, on the other object: the table pushes up on the book with 8 N.

questions.prompt: A 1000 kg car has a driving force of 500 N. Resistive forces total 200 N. Calculate the car's acceleration.
questions.solution: Resultant force $= 500 - 200 = 300$ N. $a = F \div m = 300 \div 1000 = 0.3$ m/s².

visual.alt: A 1000 kg car with a 500 N driving force to the right and 200 N resistive force to the left

questions.prompt: A resultant force of 450 N gives a motorbike and rider an acceleration of 1.5 m/s². Calculate their total mass.
In the practical to investigate how acceleration depends on force, which variable must be kept constant?
questions.solution: Only the force should change. Masses are moved from the trolley to the hanger so the total mass stays the same.
options: The total mass of the trolley and hanging masses
The acceleration of the trolley
The force on the trolley
The height of the bench above the floor

questions.prompt: What name is given to the tendency of an object to keep moving at the same velocity, or to stay at rest?
questions.solution: This tendency is called **inertia**. It is what you feel when a bus brakes and you keep going.

questions.prompt: A 1600 kg car brakes with a resultant force of 8000 N. Calculate its deceleration.
questions.solution: $a = F \div m = 8000 \div 1600 = 5$ m/s², a deceleration because it opposes the motion.

questions.prompt: The resultant force on a trolley is doubled and its mass is unchanged. What happens to the acceleration?
questions.skill: proportionality in F equals m a
questions.solution: $a = F / m$. Double $F$ with the same $m$ and $a$ doubles.
options: It quadruples
It stays the same
It halves
It doubles

questions.prompt: A 900 kg car accelerates from rest to 15 m/s in 6 s. The resistive forces total 500 N. Calculate the driving force from the engine.
questions.skill: combining a equals change in v over t with F equals m a
questions.solution: $a = 15 \div 6 = 2.5$ m/s². Resultant force $= m a = 900 \times 2.5 = 2250$ N. The driving force must also overcome the 500 N of resistance: $2250 + 500 = 2750$ N.

questions.prompt: Describe a method to investigate how the acceleration of a trolley depends on the resultant force acting on it. Include how you would make the test fair and how you would present the results.
questions.solution: Set up a trolley on a bench with a string over a pulley to a mass hanger. Put light gates along the bench connected to a data logger, or use a ticker timer, to measure the acceleration. Start with all the masses on the trolley and one on the hanger. Release the trolley and record the acceleration. Move one mass from the trolley to the hanger, so the force increases by the weight of that mass while the total mass stays the same, and repeat. Repeat each force three times and average. Plot acceleration against force; a straight line through the origin shows acceleration is directly proportional to force, and the gradient is 1 divided by the total mass. Raising the bench slightly at the pulley end can cancel friction.

questions.modelAnswer: Place a trolley on a bench and attach a string that runs over a pulley at the end of the bench to a mass hanger. Fix two light gates along the bench, connected to a data logger that calculates the acceleration of the trolley as an interrupt card passes through them. Begin with the masses on the trolley and a single mass on the hanger. Release the trolley and record the acceleration. Then move one mass from the trolley to the hanger: the force pulling the system increases by that mass's weight, but the total mass being accelerated is unchanged, which keeps the test fair. Repeat for five or six forces, taking three readings for each and averaging. Tilting the bench slightly so the trolley just rolls at constant speed with no hanging mass compensates for friction. Plot acceleration on the vertical axis against force on the horizontal axis. A straight line through the origin shows acceleration is directly proportional to force, and its gradient is 1 divided by the total mass.

questions.prompt: A cyclist of mass 70 kg rides a 10 kg bike. Pedalling gives a forward force of 200 N and resistive forces are 40 N. Show that it takes the cyclist 5 s to reach 10 m/s from rest.
questions.skill: show-that with F equals m a and acceleration
questions.solution: Resultant force $= 200 - 40 = 160$ N. Total mass $= 70 + 10 = 80$ kg. $a = 160 \div 80 = 2$ m/s². Time $= \Delta v \div a = 10 \div 2 = 5$ s, as required.

criteria.text: Uses the total mass of 80 kg: $a = 160 \div 80 = 2$ m/s²

questions.modelAnswer: The resultant force on the cyclist and bike is $200 - 40 = 160$ N forwards. The mass being accelerated is the cyclist and the bike together, $70 + 10 = 80$ kg. From $F = m a$, $a = 160 \div 80 = 2$ m/s². Rearranging $a = \Delta v / t$ gives $t = \Delta v \div a = 10 \div 2 = 5$ s. So it takes 5 s to reach 10 m/s, as required.

questions.prompt: A rocket of mass 5000 kg produces a thrust of 60 000 N at launch. $g = 9.8$ N/kg. Calculate the rocket's initial acceleration.
questions.skill: resultant with weight then F equals m a

questions.prompt: A student says: *the forces in a Newton's third-law pair are equal and opposite, so they cancel out, which means nothing could ever accelerate.* Evaluate this statement.
questions.skill: evaluating a claim about the third law
questions.solution: The student is wrong. The two forces in a third-law pair act on different objects, so they cannot cancel each other. When you push a wall with 50 N, the wall pushes you with 50 N; one force acts on the wall and the other on you. Whether you accelerate depends only on the resultant of the forces acting on *you*. Cancelling happens only between forces on the same object, which are balanced forces, not a third-law pair. So a rocket accelerates because the gas pushes on the rocket, even though the rocket pushes equally on the gas.

conclusion: the statement is wrong, confusing pairs with balanced forces

criteria.text: States that the two forces of a pair act on two different objects
Explains that forces on different objects cannot cancel

questions.modelAnswer: The statement is wrong. The forces in a third-law pair are equal in size and opposite in direction, but they act on two different objects, so they can never cancel each other out. When a swimmer pushes backwards on the water with 80 N, the water pushes forwards on the swimmer with 80 N. The force on the water acts on the water; the force on the swimmer acts on the swimmer. The swimmer's acceleration depends only on the resultant of the forces acting on the swimmer, and the 80 N forward push is unbalanced, so the swimmer accelerates. Forces only cancel when they act on the same object, and those are balanced forces, not a third-law pair. The student has confused the two ideas.

questions.prompt: A lift of mass 600 kg is pulled upwards by a cable with a tension of 7200 N. $g = 9.8$ N/kg. Calculate the acceleration of the lift.
questions.skill: resultant with weight then F equals m a
questions.solution: Weight $= 600 \times 9.8 = 5880$ N. Resultant $= 7200 - 5880 = 1320$ N upwards. $a = 1320 \div 600 = 2.2$ m/s² upwards.

examTechnique.body:
Newton's laws questions come in three shapes. A first-law question wants the sentence *resultant force is zero, so the velocity does not change*. A second-law calculation wants the resultant force found before $F = m a$ is used, with the mass of everything that accelerates. A third-law question wants a pair that is the same type, the same size, opposite in direction and on the other object, and nothing else counts.

The required practical is examined as method and as graph: say what you change, what you keep constant and how, and read the gradient as $1/m$. When a question says *estimate*, use typical values, show the steps, and round.
examinerErrors: Putting the engine force into $F = m a$ instead of the resultant force.
Using the mass of the trolley alone when the hanging masses are also accelerating.
Giving weight and the normal contact force as a third-law pair. They act on the same object.
Saying a moving object needs a force to keep it moving. It needs a resultant force only to *change* its velocity.
Adding masses to the hanger without taking them off the trolley, so the total mass changes as well as the force.
Describing the graph result as *acceleration increases with force* when the mark is for *directly proportional*, shown by a straight line through the origin.
Forgetting the direction of an acceleration found from a resultant, especially upwards for a rocket or lift.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer states which law it is using, finds the resultant force from a free body diagram before applying $F = m a$, and uses the total mass of everything that moves together. It describes the practical with the control variable named and the reason it is controlled, and reads the gradient of an acceleration-force graph as $1/m$. It identifies a third-law pair by all four features and explains why a pair can never cancel, and it produces a sensible estimate from typical speeds and times with the working shown.
